origin: cwe/94/python Remediation Steps: overriding __builtins__ is not a security mechanism, the executed code can still access all builtins

finding.name: Improper Control of Generation of Code ('Code Injection')
finding.summary: evaluate_formula runs a user-supplied formula string through eval(). Passing {'__builtins__': {}} as globals looks like a sandbox but does not remove access to Python's object introspection (for example reaching os via ().__class__.__base__.__subclasses__()), so eval() remains a code-injection sink regardless.

trap: Replacing eval() with ast.literal_eval(expression) does not work for this feature and does not close the finding: literal_eval only parses literals and a small set of container/operator forms, so it cannot evaluate an expression that references variable names, and formulas here need variables from the variables dict. A common follow-on mistake - building the expression's source text by substituting each variable's value in with str.format() or an f-string before calling literal_eval - reintroduces the same injection, because a variable's value can itself contain expression syntax that becomes part of the substituted source. The fix is to parse with ast.parse(expression, mode='eval') and walk the tree against an explicit allowlist of node types (Expression, Constant, BinOp, UnaryOp, Name restricted to keys present in variables, and the operator/unaryop base classes), rejecting anything else - not to substitute values into the expression's text.
must_preserve: evaluate_formula still returns the numeric result of formula expressions built from arithmetic operators (+, -, *, /) over names present in variables. A formula referencing a name absent from variables, or using any syntax outside arithmetic on those names, is rejected rather than evaluated.
